title: Terminology and notation
text: An Alabama county and a California school are both units, but their reports compare different outcomes. The definitions below specify what is compared, how the posterior enters the comparison, and which reports can be chosen.

title: Terminology and notation
text:
Targets and posterior uncertainty


Unit; criterion k

A unit is a firm, school, site, or other entity included in the comparison. A criterion is an outcome or other target used to evaluate the report. For example, income and incarceration are two criteria measured for the same counties.
Examples: Multiple criteria · Supplied summaries

θᵢ

The target for unit i, coded so that higher values receive higher reporting priority. The application states what higher priority means for that target.
Examples: Two-unit comparison · Alabama counties

Posterior

The distribution of target values given the data and model. Posterior risk averages the loss over this distribution. Calibration concerns how those probabilities agree with outcomes under a specified evaluation law or in new data.
Examples: Posterior shrinkage · Posterior inputs

πᵢⱼ

The posterior probability of a direction such as Pr(θᵢ > θⱼ). This calculation uses the joint distribution of the two targets because the event depends on their difference.
Examples: Direction probabilities · Interval overlap

eᵢⱼ⁽ᵏ⁾

The probability that stating i above j is wrong on criterion k. Under the zero-margin weak-error convention, equality makes either strict direction wrong. If equality has positive probability, the two directional errors sum to more than one. Each example specifies the event and any comparison margin.
Examples: Pairwise decisions · Posterior equality

Marginal interval

An interval containing a specified share of the posterior distribution for one target. A 90% interval for each of two schools gives a probability statement about each school individually. The probability that one school’s target exceeds the other’s uses their joint posterior.
Example: Report-card summaries

Expected rank

The posterior average position of a unit under a specified rank and tie convention. Ordering these averages gives one possible ranking and can define a fixed-order report family.
Example: Alternative ranking summaries

title: Terminology and notation
text:
Grade reports, disclosure and error


Common-grade report g (P1)

An ordered grouping of the units, with grade 1 at the high-priority end. The report states a direction between grades. Within a grade it leaves the comparison unstated. Using the report to allocate places or resources requires a separate rule.
Examples: Report construction · Allocation objectives

n, M

The number of included units and their M = n(n − 1)/2 unordered pairs. Each cross-grade pair contributes one stated direction.
Example: Report-family counts

N, s = N/M

The number of stated pairs and the disclosure share. The remaining M − N pairs are withheld.
Example: Disclosure from tier sizes

Eₖ

The posterior expected number of wrong stated directions on criterion k, obtained by summing directional error probabilities over the stated pairs. Joint correctness is a separate probability.
Example: Expected and realized errors

Eₖ/N

The expected wrong share among stated pairs of a fixed report. It is NA: no disclosure when N = 0.
Example: Error-rate denominators

DRₖ = Eₖ/M

The expected wrong count per possible pair. Withholding can reduce this rate by reducing the set of stated directions. The criterion subscript is usually omitted in single-criterion examples.
Example: Error-rate denominators

τ

The cost per withheld pair when a wrong stated direction costs one. Weighted risk is R_τ = (E_w + τ(M − N))/M.
Example: Reporting risk

λ, ϕ

KRW’s reward for a correct direction and the informed share in their stipulated audience model. The conversion is τ = λ/(1 + λ) and ϕ = 1 − 2τ. The positive-cost audience range is 0 < λ ≤ 1, 0 < τ ≤ 1/2 and 0 ≤ ϕ < 1. Equivalence of optimal reports requires the stated common-posterior, tie-free and common-family conditions.
Examples: Loss-scale conversion · Equivalent reporting losses



A loss-minimizing report satisfies E_w ≤ τN when the family includes the report that withholds every comparison. The inequality follows by comparing the chosen report’s loss with that benchmark. A grade report chosen by a different rule may exceed the benchmark.

title: Terminology and notation
text:
Report families and comparisons


Family; grade cap

The set of reports considered in the search. A grade cap limits the number of grades. A fixed order limits grade boundaries to cuts along that order, so the best report among those cuts may differ from the best report over all orders. Some fixed orders also keep equal scores together.
Examples: Report families · Computation methods

Frontier

The lower convex boundary of expected wrong counts plotted against disclosure for a specified report family. A point on an edge may require randomizing between complete reports. Two reports can minimize risk at the same τ while stating different numbers of pairs.
Examples: Error–disclosure frontier · Comparison constraints

ψ

The probability of choosing the report that states more pairs in a mixture of two frontier reports. Expected disclosure averages the two pair counts using the mixing probabilities. An individual draw produces one of the two complete reports.
Example: Mixtures of reports

wₖ, E_w = ∑ₖ wₖEₖ

Nonnegative criterion error weights summing to one, and the weighted expected wrong count. These weights apply to directional losses. Coefficients of a scalar composite target have a separate role.
Examples: Common grades · Composite targets

qₖ

An expected-error budget, expressed in count form as Eₖ ≤ qₖN. With no stated directions both sides are zero, although the error share is undefined. Some applications use budgets only to evaluate the displayed report; others use them to restrict selection.
Examples: Budget-constrained families · Case-report checks

Δₖ

The risk of the common report on criterion k minus the minimum risk for that criterion under the same loss and report family. If the exact minimum is unknown, bounds on it give an interval for the excess risk. Changing the loss or family changes the benchmark.
Example: Criterion-specific excess risk

Selection belief; evaluation law

The distribution used to select a report and the distribution used to evaluate that fixed report. Using a different evaluation law can change expected loss for the same grade vector.
Examples: Alternative evaluation laws · Selection-draw evaluation

Joint correctness

The probability that all stated directions are correct together. Pairwise probabilities and expected wrong counts alone do not determine this event probability. Composite targets similarly require the relevant joint-law information.
Example: Limits of pairwise probabilities

Simulation error

Numerical uncertainty due to a finite set of posterior draws. Independent draws and dependent chains require different variance calculations and diagnostics. Increasing the number of draws reduces numerical error under the supplied law without establishing the adequacy of the model.
Examples: Independent-draw error · Dependent-draw error



When repeated reports state different numbers of pairs, averaging their realized error fractions gives equal weight to reports that state at least one pair. Dividing expected wrong counts by expected stated counts gives more weight to reports that state more pairs. A posterior-reported share instead uses the probabilities supplied to that report. Averaging across reports compares these quantities, and the case-report tool specifies the denominator used in its report.

title: Terminology and notation
text:
Domain profiles and joint protection
Domain profiles give each unit a grade for each domain. The following definitions explain how those grades are compared and how joint errors enter the choice of a report.


Domain d; profile matrix G

A substantive reporting coordinate and its grade column. The matrix has units on rows and domains on columns. A common-grade report uses the same column across criteria; a multidomain profile (P2) permits separate columns. Grade 1 denotes the highest reported priority within its own domain.
Example: Common grades and domain profiles

Profile tuple; crossed directions

A unit’s ordered domain grades. Tuples such as (1,2) and (2,1) place the first unit higher in one domain and lower in the other. They do not define an overall ranking or an allocation rule. Equal grades within a domain withhold that pair’s direction without asserting equal latent targets.
Examples: Common and profile reports · Forty fictional sites

Complete joint state

A set of target values for every included unit and domain in one posterior state. A complete finite law lists each possible state and its probability. Two laws can agree within each domain and differ in how the domains vary together. Row labels on separate simulations are insufficient to recover that dependence.
Example: Dependence and joint protection

F_d, N_d, R(G)

In a joint state, F_d counts false strict directions in domain d; a strict assertion at latent equality is false. The reported card discloses N_d pairs in that domain. Its additive expected loss is R(G) = ∑_d w_d{E(F_d) + τ_d(M − N_d)}/M, with the original M = n(n − 1)/2 pair count. This expected cost is distinct from a probability that one or more protected conditions fail.
Examples: Separate weighted choices · Reporting resolution

t_d, α, J(G)

A strict false-direction-proportion threshold, an inclusive joint cap, and the direct union probability J(G) = Pr{at least one d: F_d > t_dN_d}. The union is formed within the same joint state before its probability is calculated. At N_d = 0 the ratio is not defined and the domain’s exceedance event is false. Feasibility requires J(G) ≤ α, alongside any other declared constraints.
Example: Dependence and joint protection

Separable reporting decision

An additive weighted objective whose actual feasible family factors into a Cartesian product of domain choices. Every combination of the complete weighted domain minimizer sets is then optimal in that product. Posterior independence is unnecessary. A zero-weight domain contributes every feasible column to its weighted minimizer set, while retaining its constraints. A joint constraint can prevent the feasible family from factoring.
Example: When domain choices separate

Occupied-grade counts (K_S, K_C)

The numbers of occupied grades in the two domains, rather than a particular site’s profile tuple. With a fixed law, loss and candidate bank, relaxing a budget cannot increase minimum risk. A selected domain’s grade count can nevertheless decrease as reporting detail moves to another domain. Count paths identify the canonical representative when there are tied optima.
Example: Posterior uncertainty and reporting resolution

Exact optimizer set; displayed representative

All feasible candidates that attain the same exact minimum loss. The app displays the first in a specified grade order and keeps the other tied reports available. The reported optimum is relative to the candidates included in the search.
Examples: Common versus separate columns · Dependence and tied cards

Exact calculations for a finite law

For a complete list of posterior states and probabilities, the app computes losses and tests constraints with exact fractions. A separate assessment is required if the supplied law approximates another posterior. The browser examples accept 2–4 units, 1–2 domains, 1–8 states, and at most 256 distinct profile cards, with at most 256 input columns per domain. The R package also supports assessment with independent draws and MCMC diagnostics.
Examples: Joint-law illustration · Specified reversal scenarios

Saved profiles for fictional sites

The forty-site example shows grade tuples, the settings used to choose them, and separate summaries for selection and diagnostics. The grade tuples identify occupied cells and the directions stated in each domain. Rerunning selection or computing new risk probabilities would require the original joint draws. The stored fractions describe the draws used. The diagnostic segment came from the same chain as the selection segment, so it does not provide an independent validation.
Example: Profiles of forty fictional sites

title: Alternative rankings from a posterior distribution
text: One posterior can rank units differently by posterior mean, expected rank (average position, 1st largest), and top-group probability when posteriors differ in width or skew.

title: Alternative rankings from a posterior distribution
text:
Numerical illustrations

Three-unit law, posterior mean. A has the largest mean yet the worst expected rank, 2.4 (first .3, last otherwise); 2 of the 3 pairs differ.
Three-unit law, first place. B is most likely first (.7); C never is.
Three-unit law, √θ. A’s mean falls to 1.34, below B’s 2.00 and C’s 1.73; 0 of the 3 pairs differ.
League, expected rank. Small U13 (SD .120) drops from 6th by mean to 8th by expected rank (9.59) behind U06 and U24, with 90% interval from rank 1 to rank 24; 6 of the 435 pairs differ.
League, top ten. Over 4,000 draws, U21 leads (.957) ahead of U26 (.942). Two units are never in the top ten.
League, exp(10θ). U13 climbs from 6th to 3rd by mean (4.09); 40 of the 435 pairs differ.



Sources and background

We specify the three-unit distribution and the league’s posterior directly; postrank uses these distributions as inputs. Rankings by posterior means appear in Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), Section IV.B and the notes to Figure 2C, where empirical Bayes posterior means are coarsened into deciles and quartiles; talk slide 59 sets such rules beside their grades for the firms. Their Section II.F names the expected rank.

Source: postrank theory book, ch. 25 (“Target uncertainty, directional reporting, and allocation with one place”); Kline, Rose and Walters (2024). Standalone: embed/which-ranking.html. Related: Majority wins · Ranking claims · Posterior shrinkage · Order misses.

title: Normal–normal posterior shrinkage
text: Precision weighting under a shared normal prior pulls high-SE estimates farther toward 0, reordering units only when standard errors differ.

title: Normal–normal posterior shrinkage
text:
Numerical illustrations

Prior SD .15. Small units move .640 toward 0, medium .308 and large .100 (37 of the 435 pairs reorder).
Prior SD .05. Small units move .941 and large .500 (71 of the 435 pairs reorder).
Every SE .10. Every unit keeps .692 of its estimate (0 of the 435 pairs reorder).
Against the true values. MSE falls from .0163 to .00958 and SD from .162 to .0982 (truth .149); 14 of 30 units end farther.
Too narrow a prior. At prior SD .02, MSE rises to .0197 vs. .0163 (.0191 vs. .0175 expected).



Empirical Bayes note (Kline, Rose and Walters, 2024)

Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), KRW, estimate their prior from all the firms (section III, slide 49); it is not normal, depends on each firm’s SE (section V.B) and, for race, puts all its weight on positive gaps. So State Farm’s race estimate of −.544 (SE .444) has a posterior mean of .155 (90% interval .014 to .342, from a smoothed version of KRW’s posteriors). In their data, ranks from linear (James–Stein-type) shrinkage “perform substantially worse than naively ranking the point estimates” (section V.E). The postrank theory book (ch. 26, “Empirical Bayes specification”) sets out their prior; the normal prior here is a teaching simplification. title: Expected errors in a strict ranking
text: A strict ranking of n units asserts a direction for all M = n(n − 1)/2 pairs; summing each claim’s posterior error probability 1 − πᵢⱼ gives the expected number of wrong claims.

Top 10 by posterior mean. 45 claims, 18.2 expected wrong; in Data, 5,834 California schools make 17,014,861 claims.
Six sites. 15 claims, .719 expected wrong; C above D is least certain (.362).

title: The matrix of pairwise posterior probabilities
text: Each cell gives πᵢⱼ = Pr(θᵢ > θⱼ ∣ Y), the posterior probability that row i exceeds column j (1 − πᵢⱼ across the diagonal), across alternative unit orderings.

title: The matrix of pairwise posterior probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Six sites, by posterior mean. C above D (.638) sits next to the diagonal (mirror .362); in Data, A above B (.812) and E above F (.856) follow.

title: Monte Carlo error in pairwise probabilities
text: Estimating pairwise errors from S posterior draws adds Monte Carlo noise; pairs within 2 MCSE of τ are flagged fragile, yet the coherent report need not change.

title: Monte Carlo error in pairwise probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

S 1,000. A–B is .198 vs. exact .188 (MCSE .0126; exact-e 2 MCSE ≈ .0247); capped, A and B share a grade in 100 of the 100 runs (0 of the 18 runs change).
All reports. Uncapped, the report changes in 18 of the 18 runs; in 5 more runs the estimate equals τ and 2 reports share the smallest risk (kept in 82 of 100).
S 100. MCSE .0402 (2 MCSE ≈ .0782), radius .179; exact .188 stays.
S 4,000. Radius .0283; A–B is .203 (MCSE .00636), .0116 from τ inside .0124, flagged in 54 of 100.
C–D at τ .35. C–D (exact .362) is .360 (MCSE .0240); 0 of the 35 runs change capped vs. 35 of the 35 runs uncapped.
Both scores. E–F is withheld at .202, yet fragile and stated at .192 under the first draw.



Notes on the envelope

The radius is postrank’s (postrank_iid_bounds(), no ties); the theory book’s form allows ties (4M for 2M). The envelope needs independent whole-state draws and an S fixed before drawing (an effective sample size cannot replace S in it); the MCSE shown is the IID one, as postrank_mc_fragility() computes it for independent draws (for chains it uses an MCMC MCSE). The reruns use consecutive seeds, wrapping from 4,294,967,295 back to 1 at the supported endpoint.

pr_tutorial$one$e["A", "B", "score_A"]   # 0.1883796: chance that A above B is wrong, .188 in the app

title: Marginal interval overlap and direction probabilities
text: Two marginal credible intervals can overlap substantially while the posterior of A − B strongly favors one unit having the larger true value.

title: Marginal interval overlap and direction probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Just touch, 90%. Intervals meet at 1.64 (means 3.29 SDs apart); with A − B SD 1.41 (2.33 difference SDs), Pr(A > B) = .990.
Just touch, 95%. Wider intervals touch at 3.92 SDs apart, giving Pr(A > B) = .997.
Means 2 SDs apart. Overlap 1.29 SDs, yet Pr(A > B) = .921.
Means 1 SD apart. Overlap 2.29 SDs, giving Pr(A > B) = .760.



Unequal standard deviations and source note

When two 90% intervals just touch, A is very probably the higher (.990 for independent normal posteriors with equal SDs; .997 for 95% intervals). With unequal SDs the touching distance and the SD of the difference change, and the probability changes with them. Kline, Rose and Walters (2024, section IV.C and Figure 3) draw a credible interval beside each name and assign grades from pairwise posterior probabilities.







TipIn postrank





Sites D and E of the package’s tutorial input have posterior means .15 and −.50 and SD .20 each, 3.250 posterior SDs apart: the app at ?gap=3.25 gives the same probability, .989, with intervals that overlap by .040 posterior SDs.
library(postrank); m <- postrank_posterior_means(pr_tutorial$one, level = .9)
attr(m, "upper")["E", 1] - attr(m, "lower")["D", 1]   # 0.007941451 = .040 × SD .20: the 90% intervals of D and E overlap
1 - pr_tutorial$one$e["D", "E", "score_A"]             # 0.9892219: the chance that D is truly higher

title: Posterior dependence and pairwise comparisons
text: Two units with fixed marginal posteriors can still move together. Under joint normality, correlation rescales the spread of θ_A − θ_B without changing which direction exceeds one half.

title: Posterior dependence and pairwise comparisons
text:
Numerical illustrations

Correlation .50. Difference SD narrows from .283 to .200; π_AB rises from .760 to .841.
Independent. Correlation 0 draws a circle (SD .283, π_AB = .760).
Correlation .95. Difference SD narrows to .0632; π_AB rises above .999.
Correlation −.95. Difference SD widens to .395; π_AB falls to .694.
Shared prior mean. Estimates .30, .10 (SE .20, prior SD .10, prior-mean SD .50) give ρ = .645, SD .126, π_AB = .624 (vs. .212, .575 independent); prior-mean SD 0 gives unit SDs .0894 and π_AB = .624.



Where the correlation comes from

Given the prior mean, each posterior mean keeps the share k = prior SD²/(prior SD² + SE²) of its estimate, independently. Both posterior variables depend on the uncertain prior mean, so their covariance is (1 − k_A)(1 − k_B)v, with v the prior mean’s variance given both estimates (theory book, ch. 24); with equal SEs the shared part cancels from the difference. postrank takes such posteriors as joint draws, or as normal laws averaged over the prior mean (postrank_mixture_coefficients()).

title: Reports from supplied posterior summaries
text: Paste posterior means and SDs, estimates with SEs and a stated prior, or pairwise probability matrices to build a grade report locally in your browser without uploading records.

title: Reports from supplied posterior summaries
text:
Numerical illustrations

Eight posterior summaries — 8 units with unequal precision; states 17 pairs at weighted risk .146.
Eight estimates, flat prior — posterior SD equals SE; same grades at risk .137.
Eight estimates, Normal prior — shrinks toward zero (SD .15); matches the first example at risk .146.
Two probability matrices — two criteria without marginal intervals; states 9 pairs at weighted risk .0933.
Thirty posterior summaries — searches expected-rank cuts beyond enumeration; states 251 pairs at risk .158.
All reports tied — 541 equal-risk reports (100 retained); with no pair stated, E/N is NA.



Input assumptions, validation and local exports

The normal-input calculation assumes that the units are independent given the model. Use joint draws or a joint law in R when the units are correlated. For matrices, specify the event and where the probabilities came from. The input assumes zero probability of latent equality and a zero comparison margin. The checks cover dimensions, ranges, and whether opposite directions sum to one. A joint law, calibration, and numerical accuracy need separate evidence. Leave unassessed units out of the input because a bottom grade would assert comparisons about them.
Apply keeps the previous report until the new input passes the checks. A download includes the input and settings used in the displayed report. The URL carries settings only, so paste the records and source descriptions again after a reload. If you open the optional joint solver, its status and gap describe the search using the supplied probabilities.

Open the standalone tool.

title: Report stability under repeated measurement
text: A new set of measurements can change which units a report ranks above others, even when their true values stay fixed.

title: Report stability under repeated measurement
text:
Numerical illustrations

Optimal cuts. Observation A states 251 pairs; open Data, paired measurements and repeat distribution for both refitted reports, the pair-change matrix and the replay histogram.
Estimate tiers. Fixed three-tier sizes hold disclosure at 300 pairs in both datasets while units trade grades.
Prior SD .05. A narrower assumed prior (.05) shrinks posterior means and lowers relation turnover on the same fixed truth.
Withhold every pair. Pooled E/N reads NA: no disclosure—zero turnover only because no direction is stated.
τ .05. Lowering τ to .05 prices withholding more cheaply, reducing both disclosure and relation changes.



Repeated-measurement design and notes

For each pair of measurements, we count comparisons that become stated, become withheld or reverse direction alongside the share of pairs stated and each report’s expected errors. The simulation holds the thirty true values and known standard errors fixed, draws two independent normal measurement-error vectors per pair, and computes a fresh normal posterior for each dataset under the chosen prior. Pooled claimed E/N sums expected wrong counts across both observations and divides by their total stated pairs; optimal cuts search contiguous boundaries within each dataset’s posterior-mean order.

title: Comparison at matched disclosure
text: Stating more pairs creates more chances to err. Compare each rule’s expected wrong directions with H(N), the lowest count achievable in the report family—including two-report mixtures—at that same disclosure N.

title: Comparison at matched disclosure
text:
Numerical illustrations

Same N, τ .20. Posterior-mean tiers state 21 pairs with E 3.11 against H(21) = 2.95, a gap of .163. Open Method and matched-disclosure benchmark for mixture chance .667 and the best single report at that N (E 3.013).
Estimate tiers. Three estimate tiers also state 21 pairs, leaving a larger gap of .643.
Flags. Standardized evidence flags state 19 pairs on the frontier: gap 0.
Strict order, τ .05. Stating all 28 pairs leaves gap .230, with risk above all-withheld as τ drops while the matched-N gap stays fixed.
At most three grades. Among 6,051 capped reports, three estimate tiers have gap .480 while posterior-mean tiers reach the capped endpoint.
Four tiers outside the cap. Four tiers lie outside this family (no H benchmark); all-withheld sits at N 0.



Scope and lottery notes

We evaluate all rules under the same posterior. The flags use the mean of all thirty league estimates as their reference, even when the comparison covers eight units. Each draw from a frontier lottery produces one complete report with its own disclosure count. The lottery’s error fraction divides its expected wrong count by its expected disclosure. This benchmark concerns pairwise directions under the chosen posterior and loss.







NoteIn postrank





The package’s synthetic pr_example_gaussian poverty example uses its own thirty sites. At τ .25 with at most four grades, this prints quantile cuts with N 337 and risk .1758, versus optimal cuts with N 303 and risk .1603. The risks correspond to different N; H(m) is not a package output.
library(postrank)
w <- c(poverty=1, frl=0, snap=0); s <- postrank_settings(weights=w, tau=.25, G_max=4L); sc <- pr_example_gaussian$means[, "poverty"]
sapply(c("quantile", "optimal"), function(r) unlist(postrank_cuts(sc, pr_example_gaussian, s, direction="descending", rule=r)$evaluation[c("N", "primary_risk")]))

title: Restrictions imposed by a fixed order
text: In this three-unit posterior, unit A has the largest posterior mean from a rare high-value state while B ranks first most often, so requiring grades to follow the mean order can miss the lowest-risk report.

title: Restrictions imposed by a fixed order
text:
Numerical illustrations

Mean order: τ .25. At two stated pairs, the mean-order boundary expects 7/10 wrong directions against 3/10 across all orders; the best mean-order cut withholds all pairs at risk .250 while placing B above A and C reaches .183.
Expected ranks: τ .25. Switching to expected ranks orders the units B, C, A and recovers risk .183.
Equal risk: τ .30. Reports 2/1/2 and 3/1/2 tie at the minimum risk, stating two and three pairs respectively.
Mean order: τ .50. Mean-order cuts have risk .400 against .200 for the unrestricted optimum.
Mean order: τ .10. Both methods withhold every pair at risk .100; the imposed order misses only above the cost where disclosure first pays.



Numerical illustrations and notes

The result depends on the two states and their probabilities. The cut method searches every allowed boundary within one order, whereas the joint benchmark searches every report that meets the cap. A different cap changes which reports enter the comparison. Each point on the curve compares the two methods at a common cost.

title: Coherence of pairwise threshold decisions
text: Thresholding each pair separately states a direction whenever its error probability falls strictly below τ. Compare those isolated pair choices with coherent grade reports across triples of firms.

title: Coherence of pairwise threshold decisions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Race λ .25. Naive thresholding states 1,575 directions and leaves 32,773 of 147,440 triples with two withheld pairs and one stated.
Race λ .10. The two-withheld conflict count is 24,278.
Race λ .50. Reporting more directions reduces two-withheld conflicts to 15,107.
Race λ .75. Conflicts fall further to 3,108 without any strict directed cycle.
Race λ .25, card blocks. The card withholds 575 confident pairs and states 324 directions above τ to restore coherence without a grade cap.
Gender λ 1.00. All 4,656 pairs are stated, leaving 1 directed cycle that precludes a coherent grade report.



Transitivity and archived cards

A shared grade leaves the direction between two firms unranked, and sharing a grade is transitive: withholding A–B and B–C puts all three firms in one grade, contradicting a stated direction on A–C. Threshold decisions and archived KRW cards are evaluated here under the released signed-target probabilities.

title: Standardized-evidence flags in a league
text: Grouping thirty units by standardized distance from the league mean treats an estimated reference as fixed and can rank precise lower estimates above noisy higher ones.

title: Standardized-evidence flags in a league
text:
Numerical illustrations

League, cutoff 1.96. Groups of 6, 22 and 2 state 188 of 435 pairs (E/N = .130, risk .170, 20 reversals, max error .649).
Same flags, flat prior. The same 188 pairs are evaluated under flat-prior normals around the estimates.
League, cutoff 2.576. Shrinks the outer groups and updates matrix blocks.
Same report, τ .10. Keeps 188 stated pairs while lowering all-withheld risk to τ = .10.



Reversals and individual comparison errors

At cutoff 1.96, 20 stated directions reverse the order of the estimates, and the largest error probability is .649 even though E/N lies below τ. Both matrix axes follow decreasing estimates; use the arrow keys, pointer, or Data table to inspect any pair.

title: Grades based on standardized evidence
text: Evidence flags group units by standardized distance zᵢ = (θ̂ᵢ − r)/SEᵢ from a reference r = 0, so a smaller, more precise estimate can rank above a larger one.

title: Grades based on standardized evidence
text:
Numerical illustrations

Two units, flat prior. A has z = 4.00 and B has z = 1.50, ranking A above B despite B’s larger estimate; under the flat prior, error and risk are .686.
Same flags, teaching prior. Flags stay fixed, while teaching posterior means .180 for A and .108 for B lower the error and risk to .288.
B’s SE .15. B reaches z = 2.00 and shares A’s flag, so 0 pairs are stated with risk .200.
Cutoff 2.576. The stricter cutoff separates the flags again, with error .736.



Reading the cutoff and source notes

The cutoffs 1.645, 1.96 and 2.576 are the two-sided 10%, 5% and 1% normal critical values. A flag compares one unit with the reference, whereas the probability that a stated direction between two units is right comes from the posterior.
This constructed comparator follows the postrank theory book, ch. 23 (the Tennessee procedure in ch. 2 uses a related index with other cutoffs).







TipIn postrank

title: Expected and state-specific reporting loss
text: Minimizing posterior expected loss does not guarantee winning every state: pairing two fixed reports across draws separates average risk from draw-by-draw wins.

title: Expected and state-specific reporting loss
text:
Numerical illustrations

Inside the family. Across 63 two-grade reports, the best has risk .0940 vs. .105 for tiers, yet tiers win 57 draws.
Outside the family. Three tiers reach .0417 vs. .0940 by leaving the two-grade cap.
Two-state law. Withholding has risk .250 vs. .300 for rank order, which wins with chance .700 (65 draws).
A short run. Tiers win 9 of 10 draws (mean gap −.00667).
A silent common rule. Silence has risk .200 and wrong share “NA: no disclosure.”
Identical reports. Comparing the optimum with itself gives ties 100.



Loss and sampling notes

Reporting loss adds wrong stated directions and withholding costs over all pairs, whereas the wrong fraction divides by stated pairs. Minimum expected loss applies within the searched family under the fixed posterior; paired Monte Carlo SE measures sample variation across draws.

title: Budget and grades
text:
Numerical illustrations

Tighter budget. At k=1 and cap 3/40, the unique optimum discloses A ahead only in S. Its risk is 1/5, joint-event probability 1/20, and occupied-grade counts (2,1).
Larger budget. Raising the cap to 1/8 admits the report that states a direction only in C. It has risk 11/80 and joint-event probability 1/10. With more weight on C, the best report now uses two grades in C and one in S, giving counts (1,2).
Both disclosed. At cap 3/20, the double-positive card becomes feasible at equality. Its risk is 7/80, joint-event probability 3/20, and occupied-grade counts (2,2). The cap is inclusive.
More reversals. With k=2 and cap 3/20, the best report again states a direction only in S, at risk 17/80 and joint-event probability 1/10. Changing k changes the distribution. Compare budgets within a fixed k to isolate the effect of the budget.

The chart counts the grades used in S and C. The grade table gives each site’s two grades. At every budget, the app lists all reports tied for the lowest risk and plots the counts for the first of those reports. At k=1 and zero budget, all directions are withheld at risk 1/4. At k=0, both directions can be stated even at zero budget, with risk zero.






All settings use the same nine cards, weights (1/4,3/4), and withholding costs (1/4,1/4). The joint event occurs if either domain has an error share above zero. Expected-error caps are disabled. A shared grade withholds a direction, and the error share is undefined when the report states no directions in a domain. The calculation is exact for the fictional distributions specified here.

result$summary

title: Common or profile?
text:
Numerical illustrations

Aligned priorities. Both reports place A ahead of B in both domains. Each has risk 1/10, so the difference is zero.
Crossed priorities. Under equal weights and withholding cost 1/4, the common optimum withholds both directions at risk 1/4. The profile reports A ahead in S and B ahead in C at risk 1/10. Allowing that combination reduces risk by 3/20 under the same loss.
Lower cost. At withholding cost 1/20, both reports withhold every direction. The risk is 1/20 because withholding itself carries a cost.
More weight on S. At weights 9/10 and 1/10, the common report follows S and has risk 9/50. The profile still states the crossed directions and has risk 1/10. The difference under these weights is 2/25.

With crossed priorities and equal weights, four profiles share the minimum risk of 1/10 at withholding cost 1/10. The app lists all four, including the report that withholds both directions.






The fictional distribution in each example has two states. The calculation evaluates each card under the same loss, with expected-error and joint caps disabled. A shared grade leaves the direction unstated. The results apply to the cards considered here.

title: Site profiles
text:
Numerical illustrations

Primary card. In the primary saved card, composition S has no disclosed comparisons, so its error proportion is not defined. Community C discloses 500 pairs. All forty sites occupy three profile cells.
Wider threshold. In the wider-threshold saved card (threshold 1/10), S discloses 300 pairs and C discloses 500. Their union contains 548 distinct pairs, including 16 with crossed directions. Five of six profile cells are occupied.

title: Posterior equality and withholding
text: When two true values can coincide, weak-error loss penalizes any strict direction at equality, whereas equality-neutral loss charges zero there. Assigning a shared grade withholds direction under either loss.

title: Posterior equality and withholding
text:
Numerical illustrations

Equality .40, weak loss. Withholding costs .250, below A above B (.500) and B above A (.900): equality counts against strict directions.
Equality .40, neutral loss. A above B costs .100 against withholding .150; Method lists crossings at .150 (weak) and .600, .867 (neutral).
No equality. Both losses agree and neutral all-withheld risk returns to .250.
Equality .90. B above A costs 0 while withholding costs .0250.
Certain equality. Neutral actions cost 0, the guard admits only withholding, and Data shows “NA: no distinct mass”.



Further notes on equality mass

The joint posterior assigns probability to exact equality. Equal posterior means or equal rounded observations do not establish that the targets can coincide. Each risk is specific to its own loss. The risks of withholding every pair coincide when both problems use the same action family and exact equality has zero probability for every criterion with positive weight.







TipIn postrank





The opt-in tie-aware route uses postrank_tie_pairwise() and postrank_tie_evaluate() after the law’s targets and equality declarations are supplied. Vignette m4 gives the full constructor. Its field D is the distinct mass called Q_wˢ here, and R0 is the neutral all-withheld baseline. The ordinary route requires tie-free input.

title: Reported error and reference-law evaluation
text: A grade report claims an expected wrong share under the posterior that selected it. Compare that claim with a separate reference law and the errors realized at fixed true values.

title: Reported error and reference-law evaluation
text:
Numerical illustrations

Same conditional laws. The report states 152 pair directions; both expectations equal .0632 (same prior), while the realized wrong share at fixed truth is .0526.
Narrow prior, five grades. The report claims .140 while the reference expectation is .115; their gap stays within the pair-error bound δ = .498.
Lower cost, two grades. Only 56 pair directions are stated, with claimed and reference share .0254; pairs inside each grade are withheld.
One grade, no disclosure. With 0 stated directions, every share reads “NA: no disclosure,” distinct from a defined error share of zero.



Observation replays, posterior draws, and calibration notes

Observation replays hold all true values fixed, redraw noisy estimates, and reselect a report each time. Select a replay with the slider or directly on the replay chart.
Open Data and posterior draw checks for a separate experiment that freezes the selected observations and report, then draws latent values under a declared conditional law. Chapter 18’s conditional calibration identity applies to draws from the reference law, not to replays at fixed true values; the pair-gap bound limits only the difference between the two model expectations for a fixed report.

title: Grade reports as pairwise decisions
text: Assigning sites to ordered grades states a direction for every pair in different grades and withholds every pair sharing a grade — without claiming shared-grade sites are equal.

title: Grade reports as pairwise decisions
text:
Numerical illustrations

A, then B to E, then F. States 9 of the 15 pairs (share .600) and withholds 6 inside the four-site middle grade.
Three grades of two sites. Three grades now state 12 of the 15 pairs (share .800) and withhold 3, showing how grade sizes govern disclosure.
Four sites: 1/2/2/2. States 3 of the 6 pairs (share .500). Focus a site and press a grade number, or press Enter, use Up/Down/Home/End, and press Enter to place it.

In this example, an evaluation office plans practice-documentation visits to fictional after-school sites. The grades carry no funding consequence. The exercise counts the directions in the report the reader supplies; it does not use posterior probabilities to judge whether those directions are likely to be right. title: The decision for an isolated pair
text: When exact equality has zero posterior probability, the two directions cost 1 − π_AB and π_AB, where π_AB = Pr(θ_A > θ_B ∣ Y). Withholding costs τ. The lowest line gives the best action.

title: The decision for an isolated pair
text:
Numerical illustrations

π .85, τ .10. Error e_AB = .15 exceeds τ = .10, so the lowest-cost action is to withhold.
π .85, τ .20. Raising τ to .20 lifts only the horizontal line; e_AB stays .15, selecting “state A above B”.
π .80, τ .20. At e_AB = .20 = τ, stating A above B and withholding are “equally good” at the open-circle crossing.
π .50, τ .50. All three costs equal .50, so “all three actions are equally good”.


Isolated-pair rule and multi-pair reports
With zero posterior probability of equal true values, an isolated pair discloses a direction only when its posterior probability exceeds 1 − τ (tying with withholding at equality). A shared grade withholds a direction rather than asserting equal true values; combining many pair decisions into one coherent report adds a global transitivity constraint beyond this isolated-pair rule.

title: The error–disclosure frontier
text: Plotting every grade report by stated pairs N and expected wrong directions E reveals a lower convex frontier H(m). Raising a supporting line of slope τ from below identifies the minimum-risk report at each withholding cost.

title: The error–disclosure frontier
text:
Numerical illustrations

τ .20, all reports. The touched vertex states 14 pairs with .358 expected wrong directions and risk .0372.
τ .15, all reports. A lower withholding cost selects 13 stated pairs, .169 expected wrong directions, and risk .0313.
τ .40, all reports. Costlier withholding reaches the strict order: 15 stated pairs, .719 expected wrong directions, and risk .0480.
τ .20, at most 3 grades. Among 603 capped reports, the boundary ends at 12 stated pairs with .0248 expected wrong directions and risk .0417.







Dashed segments represent random mixtures of complete reports rather than a single deterministic card. Sites are fictional tutorial data under one supplied posterior (compare Kline, Rose and Walters 2024, Section V.E, Figure 6).

p$table[, c("tau", "N", "primary_risk", "status")]

title: Restrictions on the report family
text: Minimum reporting risk depends on which grade reports are allowed: all reports, at most G grades, exactly G occupied grades, or contiguous cuts of one declared unit order.

title: Restrictions on the report family
text:
Numerical illustrations

Exactly six. Across 720 strict rankings, minimum risk is .0480 versus .0372 unrestricted.
At most three. Both the 603 capped reports and 540 three-grade reports reach .0417.
B before A. Cutting the declared order searches 32 reports at risk .0379 versus .0372.
Two criteria. Among 24 strict orders, 75 total reports, and 8 cuts, four grades cost 7/40.
A dominating set. At τ = 4/9, unrestricted optima cost 4/15 while a two-grade cap costs 17/54.



Family nesting and tie rules

At a fixed withholding cost, enlarging the allowed family can only lower the minimum risk or leave it unchanged. The dashed mark gives the risk of withholding every pair; requiring multiple occupied grades excludes that report. Equal-risk ties and the fixed-order dynamic program’s tie rule appear in Data and family search details. All examples are specified for teaching.

title: Computation of optimal grade reports
text: Enumeration scores every report in a small family, fixed-order dynamic programming cuts one declared order, and joint optimization returns an incumbent risk, lower bound and gap.

title: Computation of optimal grade reports
text:
Numerical illustrations

DP: six sites, τ .20. Among 16 contiguous reports, {A, B} > {C, D} > {E, F} achieves risk .0417, matching all 603 capped reports.
DP: inspect one cell. At step 8 of 15, the current cell chooses cut b = 2.
Twelve units. Unrestricted reports reach 28,091,567,595, capped drop to 523,251, and one order leaves 67 cuts.
A broken binary pattern. Sum 2 > 1 violates the triangle inequality: the pattern is not transitive.
Joint search: twenty units. HiGHS loads on demand for 20 league units; the four-unit example compares family risks .175 and .150.
Joint: six units. For 6 league units, 32 contiguous reports give candidate risk .146 before solving.



Model and solver notes

The six fictional sites use the postrank tutorial’s score-A normal posteriors. The solver uses independent normal posteriors for a simulated league. Its objective gives risk R = τ + Z/M. Divide an absolute objective gap by M to obtain a risk gap. A solver status or zero gap does not certify exact arithmetic or the posterior model. These distinctions follow theory chapter 14 and vignette m5. The R package selects HiGHS explicitly; Gurobi is its default backend and there is no automatic fallback.

library(postrank)
g <- c(A=1L,B=1L,C=2L,D=2L,E=3L,F=3L)
postrank_evaluate(g, pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2)$primary_risk

title: Coherence in a finite three-unit example
text: Four possible orders of A, B, and C carry fixed posterior probabilities. Evaluating all 13 coherent reports shows exact rational error and withholding costs as τ varies.

title: Coherence in a finite three-unit example
text:
Numerical illustrations

τ .20. Isolated pair choices cost 1/6 per pair, while the best coherent reports cost 11/60 and each state a direction with error 1/4.
τ .10. Placing every unit in one grade, {A, B, C}, costs 1/10 and matches the pairwise lower bound.
τ .25. Exactly 3 tied best reports reach risk 1/5 by combining different amounts of disclosure and withholding.
τ .30. Raising the withholding cost selects the full order {A} > {B} > {C} at risk 1/5 under the same fixed posterior law.



Finite-law notes

The law is set by hand for teaching, from the theory book’s three-unit example. Each bar is one complete report: its first segment is expected wrong directions per pair, and its second pays for withheld pairs. Grades decide all pairs together, so a direction with error above the price can appear in a best report. That is compatible with the report’s overall optimality. The fractions come directly from the probabilities assigned to the four states.







TipIn postrank





The package evaluates both fixed reports under these directional errors; it does not search for them. Each returns risk 11/60 at τ = 1/5. The input records the same finite teaching law used above.
e <- matrix(c(NA,1/4,1/10,3/4,NA,1/4,9/10,3/4,NA),3,byrow=TRUE,dimnames=rep(list(c("A","B","C")),2))
input <- postrank::postrank_probabilities(e,criterion="priority",event="directional_error",zero_ties=TRUE,margin=0,source=list(kind="analytic_reference",description="ABC/ACB/BAC/CBA with masses .60/.15/.15/.10",conditioning="Complete fixed finite target law"),targets=c(priority="Fictional priority; larger is higher"))
vapply(list(c(A=1,B=1,C=2),c(A=1,B=2,C=2)),function(g) postrank::postrank_evaluate(g,input,weights=c(priority=1),tau=1/5)$primary_risk,numeric(1))

title: Averaging error shares across reports
text: When stated pair counts vary across reports or datasets, the average error share depends on whether we pool counts, average over disclosing outcomes only, or impute zero for silent reports.

title: Averaging error shares across reports
text:
Numerical illustrations

Three outcomes. Pooled pairs give 2/5, disclosing outcomes give 1/2, and zero-imputation gives 1/3 (disclosure chance 2/3, mean disclosure 5/9).
More weight on errors. Increasing the error-heavy outcome’s weight shifts the pooled ratio to 4/7, the disclosing mean to 2/3, and the zero-imputed mean to 1/2.
A complete-report lottery. Mixing complete reports yields 1/8 for pooled expected counts versus 49/400 for the mean report fraction.
All silent. Both ratio-based summaries read “NA: no disclosure,” while the zero-imputed mean is 0.
Twenty datasets. Simulated league replays yield pooled error .0892 and disclosing mean .0891 against fixed true values.



Small-sample ratio note

A ratio estimated from a small sample need not be unbiased for a ratio of expectations. The hand-set outcomes provide an exact single-observation counterexample, while one trajectory of simulated datasets illustrates variability rather than repeated-sample bias.







TipIn R





A <- c(2, 0, 0); N <- c(2, 3, 0)
c(pooled=sum(A)/sum(N), disclosing=mean((A/N)[N>0]), zero_imputed=mean(ifelse(N>0,A/N,0)))

title: Minimizing the largest criterion risk
text:
Numerical illustrations

w .90 and w .70. Weighted best averages .0605 (worse endpoint .230) at .90, and .0882 (worse endpoint .138) at .70.
w .30 and Score B only. At .30 both rules select {A, B, C, D} > {E, F} (.0944); at 0 two tied weighted reports reach .200 and .211.
Book low, Book high, Book minimax, and Zero error weight. Weighted risk shifts from .250 to .150, while guarding both keeps .250 even at zero weight.
Certain opposition. Two required grades give envelope peak .500 while deterministic minimax is 1.00.



Methodological note

For the minimax calculation, we first take the expected loss on each criterion and then take their maximum. Averaging the worst loss in each posterior state would define a different decision rule. The chart clips lines that extend beyond the displayed range, while the accessible table and keyboard view retain every endpoint. Thirty sites. Across 435 pairs, 397 have opposing preferred directions, and a different site leads each criterion’s mean order.

title: Criterion-specific expected-error budgets
text: An error budget caps the expected wrong share among stated directions on each criterion. At fixed weights and withholding cost, compare the best feasible report against the unconstrained optimum.

title: Criterion-specific expected-error budgets
text:
Numerical illustrations

Loose budget. Capping score B at .03 leaves 3 reports; the unconstrained best passes at risk .0933.
Tight budget. At .02, 2 reports qualify; the best states 8 of 15 pairs at risk .0939.
Exactly three. Requiring three grades at .02 leaves 0 reports feasible because full withholding is excluded.
Both budgets. Capping each score at .02 leaves 2 reports passing both count-form checks.
Zero weight. Score B has zero loss weight yet keeps its .10 cap: risk .0906, average share .0267, largest error .240 (in Data).
No budget. Optimizing score A alone lowers risk to .0417 while raising score B’s wrong share to .237.



Model notes

The example uses independent normal posteriors for six fictional sites. Each budget limits the posterior expected share over stated directions rather than individual pair probabilities. A report that withholds every pair has expected wrong count and stated count equal to zero, so it satisfies homogeneous count-form budgets whenever the grade cap permits it, while its error share is undefined (NA: no disclosure).

Weighted report. Report 1/1/1/1/2/3 has risk .0933 from contributions .0453 and .0480.

TipIn postrank





The fixed default report reproduces the two calculations; small floating-point rounding differences do not change their algebraic identity.
library(postrank)
ev <- postrank_evaluate(c(A=1L,B=1L,C=1L,D=1L,E=2L,F=3L), pr_tutorial$two, weights=c(score_A=.5,score_B=.5), tau=.2)
sum(c(.5,.5)*ev$criterion_risk); ev$weighted_risk





Mixture independence and KRW correspondence

The criterion draw is independent of the targets conditional on the supplied information, with probabilities given by the loss weights. In postrank, a strict direction counts as wrong when target values are equal. Correspondence to KRW’s strict-count objective requires matching the law, targets, orientation, units, and report family, plus the affine and equality conditions of that result.

title: Composite targets and criterion directions
text: Weighting directional errors across criteria and ordering a weighted composite of their values can select opposite directions for the same pair.

title: Composite targets and criterion directions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Different targets. Criterion costs .250, .750, .300 vs. composite costs 1.00, 0, .300 pick 1/2 and 2/1.
Rescale the second criterion. In Data and exact values, A’s composite becomes .250 and flips direction.
Composite equality. Strict composite directions cost 1.00 vs. .300 to withhold; sharing a grade withholds.
Two reports, same disclosure. Across 75 reports in Data and exact values, criterion picks 1/2/2/3 (.142) and composite picks 1/1/2/3 (.0333), each stating 5 pairs.
Transform the whole law. Exponentiating keeps criterion risk .142 while moving composite to 1/1/2/2 (.0667).
Rescale the Normal composite. Independent Normal margins give first-site composite mean .635.



Weights, rescaling, and synthetic laws

Error weights set the cost of wrong criterion directions, whereas nonnegative composite coefficients summing to one combine magnitudes into a new target. A positive multiplier rescales a criterion inside the composite, while any strictly increasing whole-law transformation leaves criterion orderings intact. All examples use synthetic supplied laws; marginal-only releases leave cross-criterion dependence undetermined.







TipIn postrank





The code computes composite scores from the posterior means, with weights as the composite coefficients. The package divides by the supplied scale, so a second-criterion scale of ten corresponds to a multiplier of .1.

title: KRW’s reward and postrank’s withholding cost
text: KRW award λ for a correct direction and zero for withholding, whereas postrank charges τ for withholding; under common tie-free assumptions, τ = λ/(1 + λ) selects the same reports.

title: KRW’s reward and postrank’s withholding cost
text:
Numerical illustrations

λ .25 (KRW’s card) gives τ .20 and pair cutoff .80; both rules choose {A} > {B} > {C, D} > {E} > {F}.
λ .08 gives τ .0741 and tightens the pair cutoff, leaving fewer comparisons stated.
λ .10 gives τ 1/11, cutoff 10/11, and best report {A, B} > {C, D} > {E, F}.
λ .50 gives τ 1/3 and pair cutoff 2/3 across the reverse- and forward-direction lines.
λ 1 gives τ .50 and full order {A} > {B} > {C} > {D} > {E} > {F} where the two cuts meet.
τ .40 sets λ to 2/3 from the withholding-cost scale.



Scope and audience-model notes

The conversion changes the scale of the loss under the same posterior and feasible family. It supplies no evidence about posterior calibration. A grade report must give transitive directions, so an isolated pair’s cutoff cannot serve as a separate constraint on each reported direction. The audience share comes from the assumptions in KRW’s behavioral model. The example contains no observations of readers.

title: A high-probability school comparison withheld
text: The minimum-risk three-grade report puts F and I in the same grade despite strong posterior evidence for F above I.

title: A high-probability school comparison withheld
text:
Numerical illustrations

F above I. Probability is above .999; across 175,099 reports stating it, best risk is .0641 (optimum .0638).
I above F. Requiring the reverse direction raises minimum risk to .112.
The tertiles state it. Tertile cuts state 48 pairs at risk .0823, stating F above I in three grades.
The higher-cost optimum. At τ = .45, the optimum states F above I at risk .143.



Family restrictions and scope notes

Requiring F above I can change comparisons involving other schools, so the browser searches the three-grade family again with that direction required. In Method, a four-grade dynamic-programming search along the posterior-mean order admits reports that the three-grade search excludes while excluding non-monotone groupings; both use the same posterior, τ, and weight, so their risks are directly comparable. A shared grade leaves relative chronic absence unstated. This twelve-school teaching subset is conditional on a statewide prior fitted to 5,834 eligible schools (prior-estimation uncertainty is not propagated). One boundary. Position 6 gives two grades, 36 pairs, and risk .0913.

Scope and Dashboard notes

Moving a cut changes both how many comparisons the report states and which schools it compares. Numerical illustrations

Cohort scope and commonality notes

Opportunity Atlas estimates pool race and gender for 1978–83 birth cohorts with parents at the 25th income percentile (household income in 2014–15; incarceration on April 1, 2010). With posterior, criterion weight, and the three-grade family held fixed, increasing τ never reduces the total number of stated pairs in an exact optimum, yet moving a whole block boundary can newly withhold pairs stated earlier or state pairs whose individual error exceeds τ. Data lists every changed pair, equal-risk boundary ties within numerical tolerance, and the 13 archived HiGHS runs alongside the browser’s exact enumeration. A shared grade leaves relative chronic absence unstated. This twelve-school teaching subset is conditional on a statewide prior fitted to 5,834 eligible schools (prior-estimation uncertainty is not propagated). title: Equivalent reporting-loss scales
text: Scoring all 4,683 six-site reports by KRW’s loss at λ and by postrank’s risk at τ = λ/(1 + λ) relates both objectives by an increasing affine transformation.

title: Equivalent reporting-loss scales
text:
Numerical illustrations

τ .25, whole grid checks 49 values of τ; both objectives return the same best-report set at 49 of 49 values.

Numerical illustrations

Equal weights. Excess risks are .0490 on score A and .0145 on score B, joining each criterion’s own minimum to its common-report risk.

title: Opposing criterion directions
text: Criteria favor opposite directions for a pair when each assigns smaller error to a different strict order. Compare standalone directional costs, withholding cost, and criterion-specific errors.

title: Opposing criterion directions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Six sites, B–C. Standalone costs are .484 (B above C) and .516 (C above B), among 3 opposing pairs.
Thirty sites. Across 397 opposing pairs, the selected pair’s smaller expected directional cost is .365.
Certain opposition. Strict directions cost .500 while withholding costs .200, matching within-state conflict.

Strict ranking statements count latent equality as wrong, so comparing each error probability with its reverse identifies a criterion’s preferred direction even when both exceed one half. title: Error budgets under estimated pairwise probabilities
text: A report meeting an error budget under estimated pair probabilities can fail under the exact posterior. A uniform error margin ε brackets exact feasibility between inner and outer sets.

text: Pairwise probabilities fix a report’s additive expected risk, whereas composite directions and joint all-correct probabilities depend on how errors occur together.

title: Quantities not identified by pairwise probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Together: Additive risk and all-criteria correctness are both .500 when the criteria agree across states.

Changing how the two criteria’s states are paired while holding each criterion’s two-unit distribution fixed leaves every fixed report’s additive risk invariant. Joint all-criteria correctness and composite directions still move because composite targets depend on magnitudes and joint events depend on whole-state probabilities. Larger target values indicate higher reporting priority; marginal pair probabilities alone leave joint events and composite posteriors undetermined.

title: Evaluation under an alternative posterior law
text: A report chosen under one posterior law can be evaluated under another. Holding that selected report fixed, evaluation regret measures how far its evaluation-law risk sits above the evaluation-law optimum.

title: Evaluation under an alternative posterior law
text:
Numerical illustrations

Same laws. Risk is .0417 under either law, and evaluation regret is 0.
Move C upward. Fixed-report evaluation risk rises to .136 against evaluation-best .0542: regret .0817 and 3 changed pairs.
Wider evaluation law. Evaluation risk rises to .0779, yet regret stays 0 because the same report stays best.

Small change, new report. With 1 changed pair, How the bounds are calculated gives radius .0132 and regret .000755 below .0263.



Further notes on discrepancy bounds

Both laws use independent normal distributions specified for the example. The regret bound adds two quantities: twice a uniform bound on the difference in risks across laws and a bound on the selection-law optimization gap. Both bounds apply to the whole common family. We enumerate every report, so the selection-law optimization gap is zero. Increasing the number of draws under either law would leave any difference between the two laws in place.

title: Coherence constraints on pairwise decisions
text: Choosing the lowest-loss action for each pair separately need not yield a valid grade report. Moving middle firm B’s posterior mean shows when coherence adds risk.

title: Coherence constraints on pairwise decisions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Middle at 1.00. Isolated pairs withhold A–B and B–C while stating A above C (probability .921). Shared grades are transitive, so the best coherent reports reach risk .173.
Middle at .50. B sits closer to C, so the pairwise choices print directly as {A} > {B, C} at risk .141.
Middle at .80. Just below the shaded band, the pairwise choices still print as one report at risk .159.
Middle at 1.00, τ .10. Lowering the withholding cost shifts the best coherent report to {A, B, C} at risk .100, withholding the confident outer pair too.
Middle at 1.00, τ .25. The threshold drops to .75, below .760, so every pair is stated as {A} > {B} > {C} and the incoherent band disappears.



Transitivity and scope notes

Sharing a grade is transitive. If A shares a grade with B and B with C, the report must also withhold the comparison of A and C. Kline, Rose and Walters describe the conflict with the separate pair decisions as a “Condorcet cycle in indifferences.” These are posteriors set by hand for teaching. The badge “E ≤ τN applies” appears only for an exact optimum of the shown family when that family includes the all-withheld report; for any other report the badge states only whether E ≤ τN holds (R ≤ τ). Six-site draws sample independent normal latent values (Monte Carlo all-right estimates), whereas the three-unit law gives exact joint probabilities and union lower bounds (postrank theory book, chapters 10 and 15). text: Randomizing between two frontier corner reports achieves any intermediate mean number of stated pairs along H(m), often with far fewer expected wrong directions than any single report at that disclosure.

title: Mixtures of frontier reports

Numerical illustrations

Six sites, mean 10. Mixing the 12-pair report (chance .50) and the 8-pair report yields .0171 expected wrong directions; no single report states this count.

title: Sensitivity to corrections and unit removal
text: Grades are assigned jointly, so correcting one unit’s posterior—or removing a unit—can move grade boundaries and change reported relations between units whose posteriors stayed fixed.

title: Sensitivity to corrections and unit removal
text:
Numerical illustrations

Correct a mean. Lowering C changes 2 of 10 untouched pairs (D–E, E–F).

The example uses independent normal posteriors and changes only the selected marginal; refitting a model to corrected data could also move other marginals. title: Reporting risk and withholding cost
text: A wrong stated direction costs 1 and withholding a pair costs τ. Posterior risk R_τ = E/M + τ(M − N)/M averages expected mistakes and withheld comparisons across all M pairs.

title: Reporting risk and withholding cost
text:
Numerical illustrations

τ .20, at most 3 grades. The best of 603 reports states 12 of 15 pairs (risk .0417); 2 (A and B; E and F) below-τ pairs stay withheld because the grade cap links pairwise decisions.
τ .20, no cap. The best of 4,683 reports states 14 of 15 pairs (risk .0372), withholding only C–D.
τ .40, no cap. The strict order states 15 of 15 pairs (risk .0480, entirely expected mistakes).
τ .30, no cap. The optimal report is unchanged while its risk becomes .0438; open Score your report to evaluate any fixed grade vector beside it.



Model assumptions and source notes

We use the normal posteriors for score A at six fictional sites from the postrank tutorial. For these posteriors and the costs on the slider, the uncapped optimum states the pairs whose error is below τ. Posterior risk is an expected cost per pair; the chance that at least one direction is wrong is a separate joint probability (postrank theory book, chapters 10–11).







TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
g <- c(A=1L,B=1L,C=2L,D=2L,E=3L,F=3L)
postrank_evaluate(g, pr_tutorial$one, weights=c(score_A=1), tau=.2)$primary_risk
This scores the displayed capped report directly. The package’s solver-based tutorial also reports a floating-point correction to the lower bound; direct fixed-report evaluation needs no solver.

title: Posterior summaries in a grade report
text: Each row plots a unit’s posterior mean and marginal interval in its grade’s color. Cross-grade pairs state a direction; same-grade pairs are withheld; below-diagonal cells average cross-grade error probabilities.

title: Posterior summaries in a grade report
text:
Numerical illustrations

Six sites. The card states 12 of 15 pairs (share .800), with risk .0417 and expected share wrong .00206. Adjacent-grade cells show .0024 and .0038; the diagonal marks withheld pairs.
Reveal by grade. Only Grade 1 is drawn first, and the matrix notes “With one grade shown there is nothing to compare yet.” Revealing later grades adds their cross-grade cells.
Thirty sites. The card states 303 of 435 pairs, with risk .160 and expected share wrong .121. Adjacent-grade shares are .2019, .1672 and .0640.


Sorting within grades and marginal intervals
Expected rank averages a unit's position under the posterior, with the top position first. Sorting by posterior mean can rearrange rows within a grade while keeping same-grade comparisons withheld and preserving the report's risk. These synthetic posteriors are taken as given; Grade 1 declares priority (highest synthetic need in the poverty example). Each interval describes one unit alone, and overlap does not determine grades. The larger example restricts its search to contiguous cuts of the expected-rank order from the poverty criterion of pr_example_gaussian; the card follows the package's report-card plot and the between-grade table follows Figure 10 and Section VI.B of Kline, Rose and Walters.

title: Optimal reports along the withholding-cost path
text: Each fixed report’s posterior risk is a straight line in τ whose slope is the share of withheld pairs. The lower envelope traces the minimum-risk report across τ, bending wherever the optimal report changes.

title: Optimal reports along the withholding-cost path
text:
Numerical illustrations

Overview. The unrestricted optimum states 14 pairs (risk .0372), compared with .0417 under the three-grade cap. Open Complete path for exact intervals.
Before the first bend. The report states 0 of 15 pairs, with withholding cost .0005.
Small cost, coherent report. The optimum states 12 of 15 pairs, including 2 directions whose error exceeds τ because grades are chosen jointly.
Exactly at a bend. At τ ≈ .144, 2 reports share the smallest risk where neighboring segments meet.
Three-grade cap. At τ = .40, the capped report states 12 of 15 pairs (risk .0817) while the unrestricted optimum reaches .0480.

The six fictional site posteriors are normal and specified for teaching. An independent three-unit equal-mean example illustrates reports that minimize risk only at a single endpoint τ = .50 without occupying an interval of positive length.

title: Error rates under two denominators
text: Both error rates divide the same expected wrong count E by different pair totals: KRW’s discordance rate DR = E/M uses all M pairs, while E/N uses the N stated pairs.

title: Error rates under two denominators
text:
Numerical illustrations

τ .25. Stating 14 of 15 pairs (share .933) gives DR .0238 and E/N .0255; the two rates stay close when almost all pairs are stated.
KRW setting. KRW’s race card states 1,324 of 4,656 pairs (share .284), shrinking E/N .136 to DR .0387 (KRW risk −.0227, postrank risk .1818).
All pairs stated. Stating all 15 pairs makes both denominators equal, so DR and E/N both equal .0480 while the archived card stays fixed.


Rounding and archived card probabilities
For positive N, DR = (N/M) × E/N; rounded displays use an approximation sign when multiplying rounded shares does not reproduce the rounded product. Both rates are expectations over pairs, whereas the chance of at least one error depends on the joint distribution. KRW's archived card statistics and the evaluation on released pair probabilities agree at the displayed digits; we evaluate the archived grade assignments under postrank's loss.

title: Domain profiles
text:
Multiple criteria → Domain profiles
Domain profiles give sites a separate grade for each outcome. A site can rank higher on composition need and lower on community need. The two grades describe those separate priorities.
P.1 compares common and separate grades. P.2 considers when grades can be chosen separately, P.3 examines errors that overlap across domains, and P.4 varies the budget for errors across both domains.
The first four examples evaluate every candidate under a fully specified fictional distribution. The forty-site example shows grades and risk summaries from an earlier fictional analysis.

title: Error overlap
text:
Numerical illustrations

Coincident. The two directions each have error probability 1/10, and they fail together. Stating both gives probability 1/10 of at least one error, below the cap 3/20. That card alone minimizes expected loss at 1/10.
Disjoint failures. The marginal probabilities remain 1/10, but the probability of at least one error rises to 1/5 if the report states both. The cap rules out that card. Two cards tie at risk 7/40, each stating one positive direction and withholding the other.
Independent. At overlap c=1/100, the probability of at least one error when stating both is 19/100. This exceeds the joint cap even under independence, so the same two cards tie for the lowest risk.
At joint cap. At c=1/20, the probability of at least one error when stating both is exactly 3/20. A probability equal to the cap is allowed, so that card is feasible and uniquely optimal.







The example uses a complete fictional distribution with equal domain weights, withholding cost 1/4, and zero thresholds. The joint event occurs if either domain’s error share exceeds its threshold. A shared grade leaves a direction unstated. When several feasible cards have the same lowest risk, the app lists all of them and shows one first. The exact calculation applies to this distribution and these candidates.









TipIn postrank





The R script reproduces the example with postrank 1.2.0 and gmp.
source("profile-dependence.R")
result <- profile_dependence()
result$summary



Source: postrank multidomain decisions.

title: Separate or joint?
text:
Multiple criteria → Domain profiles
Standalone: open this app, for example ?preset=independent-joint&theme=dark.
Related applications: Common or profile? and Error overlap.

title: Separate or joint?
text:
Numerical illustrations

Separate choices. Coincident reversals give a feasible product of all nine cards. Both domains prefer A ahead, with total risk 1/10, even though their targets are dependent.
Same minimum. Disjoint reversals leave each domain’s distribution and weighted losses unchanged. With the joint cap disabled, stating A ahead in both domains still gives the unique optimum at risk 1/10.
Zero S weight. All three S columns have the same weighted loss, and C still favors A ahead. The three resulting cards tie at risk 1/10. Their unweighted losses in S differ.
Independent, cap. With independent domains under the joint guard, the feasible family has three cards and fails the product condition. The two domain minima sum to 1/10, but the card that combines them has joint-event probability 19/100, above the cap 3/20. The two feasible optima each state a direction in one domain, at risk 7/40.
Coincident, cap. Under the joint guard with coincident failures, four feasible cards form a product of two columns per domain. The best card states A ahead in both domains. Its risk and joint-event probability are both 1/10.

With independent reversals, zero S weight, and an active cap, a feasible card still reaches the lower bound of 1/10. Some combinations of weighted minima exceed the cap, but only one needs to pass to reach the bound. Errors in S still count toward the cap when its loss weight is zero.






The fictional distributions have the same marginals. The calculation evaluates the nine cards in this example, with expected-error caps disabled and the joint cap set separately. A shared grade leaves the direction unstated. If the supplied law approximates another posterior, feasibility under that posterior requires a separate check.









TipIn postrank





The R script reproduces all twelve settings with postrank 1.2.0 and gmp. It uses the public results to identify each domain’s feasible columns and weighted minima.

result$summary

title: Deciles and quartiles of posterior means
text: Quartiles and deciles split firms into nearly equal posterior-mean groups, keeping exact score ties together. Compare these fixed tiers with KRW’s archived cards on discordance and informativeness.

title: Deciles and quartiles of posterior means
text:
Numerical illustrations

Race quartiles, card λ .60. Quartiles sit at DR .170 and I .419; the ringed card reaches lower DR (.168) and higher I (.434).
Race deciles, card λ .82. Deciles move to DR .227 and I .455, while the selected card reaches .224 and .459.
Gender quartiles, card λ .64. Under the signed male-name contact-gap target, quartiles give DR .198 and I .362; the card gives .191 and .388.
Gender deciles, card λ .80. Deciles give DR .252 and I .404; the card gives .237 and .408. Not every λ improves both axes.



Reporting axes and archived-card provenance

KRW discuss deciles and quartiles in §IV.B (Figure 2C) and reporting possibilities in §V.E (Figure 6). The diamonds show the fixed tiers, while the curve joins cards that KRW selected using their archived probabilities. Here each card’s coordinates are recomputed under the released signed-target probabilities without rerunning that search. KRW write τ̄ for informativeness.

title: Fixed quantile tiers
text: A quantile-tier rule cuts estimate order into nearly equal groups, ranking higher tiers above lower tiers and withholding same-tier pairs. Posterior probabilities evaluate its expected wrong directions and reporting risk.

title: Fixed quantile tiers
text:
Numerical illustrations

Three tiers. Three groups of 10 state 300 of 435 pairs (.690). Under the teaching posterior, expected wrong directions are 51.9 (.173 per stated pair) and risk is .181 at τ = .20.
Ten tiers, marks on. Disclosure rises to 405 pairs (.931), while expected wrong directions rise to 89.4 (E/N = .221) and risk to .219; 197 stated pairs have error above τ (largest .802).
Four tiers. Quantile positions give sizes 8, 7, 8, 7 and state 337 pairs (.775); Method and formulas shows the grouped binomial count without the equal-size shortcut.
Two tiers. Two groups of 15 state 225 pairs (.517), leaving two within-tier triangles along the diagonal.
Thirty tiers. Stating all 435 pairs in estimate order expects 102 wrong directions; with a single tier, E/N becomes “NA: no disclosure” and risk is .200.



Simulation and tie-handling notes

The example uses one set of estimates for thirty simulated units and independent normal posteriors based on a prior with mean 0 and SD .15. Changing τ alters the reporting loss and which stated pairs exceed τ without moving tier membership. In Ranking states many claims, ranking by posterior means rather than raw estimates changes the expected wrong count. If an exact tie spans two tiers, postrank merges those tiers to keep tied units together.

title: Reporting rules
text: Tiers, evidence flags and cuts of a ranking all place some units above others and leave some pairs unranked. We compare their pairwise directions using the same posterior and loss. Other examples examine stability under repeated measurement and the additional choices needed for allocation and classification.

title: Reporting, allocation and classification
text: A grade report states pairwise directions; filling fixed places or classifying above a threshold optimizes a separate objective and needs its own rule.

title: Reporting, allocation and classification
text:
Numerical illustrations

Three units, reporting objective. Risk is .183; Grade 1 picks B for value 4.00 and overlap .700, whereas mean-value order picks A for 6.00 and .300 (risk .467).
Two units, τ .25. Boundary lottery gives value 5.00 and overlap .500.
False-negative cost 3. Bayes picks 2 positive at cost .700 vs. .900 for Grade 1; at Threshold 4, Bayes picks 0 at cost .300.
Equal reporting risk, different classifications. Reports 2/1/2 and 3/1/2 tie at risk .200, yet grades ≤ 2 pick 3 vs. 2 positive at costs 1.70 vs. 1.30.
League, five places. Mean order gives value .558 and overlap 2.73; top-set order reaches 2.83.



Exact laws and league approximations

Value denotes selected target value. Finite-law quantities are exact; league means and threshold probabilities are analytic while top-set membership and overlap use Monte Carlo draws. The league’s reporting optimum searches contiguous posterior-mean cuts under a grade cap.

title: Tiers and optimized cuts of posterior rankings
text: Fixed quantile tiers set boundaries by group size; optimal cuts adjust those boundaries while keeping the posterior order fixed.

title: Tiers and optimized cuts of posterior rankings
text:
Numerical illustrations

Eight units: optimal cuts. Mean-order and rank-order cuts state 17 pairs at risk .146, matching the best of 6,051 reports; tiers state 21 at .161.
League: fixed tiers. Tiers state 300 pairs at risk .173; mean-order cuts state 251 at .158.
Thirty sites: rank cuts. Rank cuts state 303 pairs at risk .160 across 4,090 contiguous reports.
Eight units: all reports. Searches all 545,835 reports.



Numerical illustrations and notes

When the quantile boundaries are among the allowed cuts of an order, the minimum over those cuts cannot have higher risk than the quantile report. Searching other orders may yield a lower minimum within the grade cap. The comparison also depends on the objective: a cut that minimizes directional error can differ from one that minimizes error on a composite score. We do not estimate the gap to the joint optimum for the larger examples.







TipIn postrank





library(postrank)
w <- c(poverty = 1, frl = 0, snap = 0); s <- postrank_settings(weights = w, tau = .25, G_max = 4L)
pm <- postrank_cuts(pr_example_gaussian$means[, "poverty"], pr_example_gaussian, s, direction = "descending", method = "posterior_mean")
c(risk = pm$risk)
