title: Common withholding cost and matched disclosure
text: Rules that disclose different numbers of pairs can be compared two ways: by total risk at a common withholding price τ, or by expected wrong directions at matched disclosure N under one posterior.

title: Common withholding cost and matched disclosure
text:
Numerical illustrations

Same τ, .20. Posterior-mean tiers state 21 pairs with risk .161, while the best report states 17 pairs with risk .146.
Same N, eight units. At matched disclosure N 21, posterior-mean tiers leave excess-error gap .163 above H(21).
Thirty units, one order. Among 436 three-grade cuts, posterior-mean tiers state 300 pairs with E 48.3 on the order boundary.
Thirty units, same τ. Without the grade cap, the order family spans 536,870,912 contiguous cuts of the posterior-mean order.
Flags outside the order. Evidence flags lie outside this family: risk is still evaluated, without an order-family benchmark.
All-withheld. Disclosing 0 pairs gives risk .200 at τ .20, with undefined wrong share among stated pairs.



Scope and posterior notes

We evaluate the rules under the same normal posterior. The flags use the mean of all thirty estimates as their reference. For thirty units, the boundary comes from the hull of contiguous cuts in the given order. The withholding cost determines the loss, and the report family determines which benchmarks are available. An allocation or classification decision would require its own objective.







NoteIn postrank





The package’s synthetic pr_example_gaussian poverty example uses its own thirty sites. At τ .25 with at most four grades, this prints quantile cuts with N 337 and risk .1758, versus optimal cuts with N 303 and risk .1603. The risks correspond to different N; H(m) is not a package output.
library(postrank)
w <- c(poverty=1, frl=0, snap=0); s <- postrank_settings(weights=w, tau=.25, G_max=4L); sc <- pr_example_gaussian$means[, "poverty"]
sapply(c("quantile", "optimal"), function(r) unlist(postrank_cuts(sc, pr_example_gaussian, s, direction="descending", rule=r)$evaluation[c("N", "primary_risk")]))

title: Disclosure determined by tier sizes
text: Tier sizes alone determine how many pairs are ranked across tiers and how many stay unranked within tiers. Holding unit and tier counts fixed, the distribution weights every nonempty ordered size pattern equally.

title: Disclosure determined by tier sizes
text:
Numerical illustrations

Balanced thirty. Sizes 10, 10, 10 state 300 of 435 pairs (.690), attaining the maximum disclosure for three tiers.
Two tiny tiers. Sizes 1, 1, 28 state only 57 pairs against the balanced maximum of 300; reordering those sizes yields another pattern with the same disclosure.
Four tiers. Sizes 8, 7, 8, 7 state 337 pairs (.775), the maximum for four tiers of thirty units.
Balanced twelve. Three groups of four state 48 of 66 pairs; open Settings to edit the size vector or individual tiers.
Unbalanced twelve. Sizes 5, 4, 3 state 47 pairs, below the balanced maximum of 48.



Composition weights and tie notes

The distribution includes every ordered size pattern with at least one unit per tier. Each pattern is counted once regardless of how many ways units could be assigned to it. Quantile rules usually produce nearly balanced sizes, although postrank can merge neighboring tiers to keep equal estimates together. Assessing accuracy requires unit assignments and pairwise posterior error probabilities in addition to tier sizes.

text: Build a grade report from released case probabilities, check error budgets on the displayed grades, and export the model sentence, CSV tables, and R verification script.

title: Case-report specification and export
text:
Numerical illustrations

CDE: three-grade family. Enumerates 523,251 capped reports; states 45 pairs.
KRW: equal weights. Labeled “optimal within this order”; states 636 pairs.
Alabama: equal weights. States 1,249 pairs; Grade 1 marks favorable outcomes, not need.
CDE: cap two. Searches 4,095 reports; compare with the archived solve in Data.
CDE: mean-order cap four. Uses the posterior-mean order and checks error budgets.

NoteIn postrank





The mean-order cap-four result states 54 pairs, with risk .0368858. Run the example with postrank 1.2.0 and its bundled CDE data.
library(postrank)
x <- pr_case_cde$input; s <- postrank_settings(weights = c(negative_chronic_absence = 1), tau = .2, G_max = 4)
a <- postrank_cuts(x$summaries$means[, 1], x, s, direction = "descending", rule = "optimal")
a$evaluation[c("N", "E_over_N", "primary_risk")]





Scope, sources, and CSV conventions

The archived status, bound, and gap apply to the archived computation. The current search has its own scope. A shared grade leaves the comparison unstated. The expected error share describes individual comparisons in aggregate, and the probability that every stated comparison is correct requires a joint calculation. A decision to allocate resources would require a further rule. Draft text stays in the open component’s memory.
CDE uses the fitted statewide prior. KRW uses historical contact-gap estimates from Kline, Rose and Walters and their data deposit, under the deposit’s CC-BY-NC terms (no version stated). The experiment describes historical contact gaps. Alabama uses Opportunity Atlas historical outcomes under CC BY 4.0. The case notes and downloads give the source, changes, rights, and conditioning. These details appear on each CSV row. Relations use 1 for row above column, -1 for column above row, 0 for withheld, and NA on the diagonal.

title: Marginal summaries and joint direction probabilities
text: Outside a jointly normal posterior, marginal means no longer settle π_AB = Pr(θ_A > θ_B ∣ Y): identical margins can reverse π_AB from 1/3 to 2/3, and skewness can flip mean against direction.

title: Marginal summaries and joint direction probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Law 1. Uniform 1/3 margins (means 1.00) give π_AB = 1/3, π_BA = 2/3; at w = .20, A’s mean .120 exceeds B’s 0 while π_AB = .392.
Law 2. Re-pairing the same margins raises π_AB to 2/3.
Independent. Every pair once: margins stay 1/3 with tie probability 1/3, so π_AB = π_BA = 1/3 (sum 2/3).
Always equal. Same margins, with A always equal to B (π_AB = π_BA = 0).
w .50. Equal bump weights give mean .450 and π_AB = .620; open Method and details for the flip range (.10 to .30).


Model assumptions and source notes
The joint laws follow the postrank theory book, ch. 9 (Fig. f09b). Tie-freeness (θA ≠ θB) is a joint-law property; postrank_mixture_coefficients() averages within-component pair probabilities by mixture weights.

Standalone: embed/beyond-normal.html (?cells=021100010&mixW=.30 or ?preset=law2&theme=dark). Related: 1.8 and 1.9.
Theory book · Dependence and pairwise comparison probabilities.

title: Monte Carlo error with dependent draws
text: Correlated Markov chain draws carry less information about π_AB than independent draws, inflating estimator variance so nominal independence-based error bounds fail far too often.

title: Monte Carlo error with dependent draws
text:
Numerical illustrations

Stay .99. Naive iid SD is .0500 vs. exact .376; the .05 iid bound (±.148) fails in 1,602 of the 2,000 chains (.801; exact .804), at least .370 from never switching.
Stay .99, chain-aware. Exact SD is .376 (variance .141) vs. .0500 (.00250) iid, matching 1.77 independent draws (long-run 1.01).
A stuck chain. Chain 7 never switches; 720 chains never switch.
Stay .50. Independent draws fail in 10 of the 2,000 chains (.00500; exact .00352).
1,000 draws. Precision equals 10.6 independent draws; the ±.0468 bound fails in .777 of chains (exact .770).
postrank’s chains. Open Data: pr_toy_mcmc gives share .172 vs. .2 (MCMC MCSE .0576 vs. .00835 iid; R-hat 1.0905, ESS 42.95) and loss .248 vs. 4/15 (.191 to .296 by chain).


Source and package notes
The stationary two-state chain with $\pi_{AB} = 1/2$ is restated from the postrank theory book, ch. 21 (“A finite-sample coefficient bound for dependent draws”); exact finite-sample variances and tail probabilities follow from the transition probability alongside outcomes counted across chains simulated in the browser. In postrank, postrank_iid_bounds() refuses MCMC draws, and postrank_diagnose() reports R-hat, ESS and an MCMC MCSE for them (vignette m6, “Monte Carlo uncertainty and diagnostics”).

mc <- postrank_draws(pr_toy_mcmc, regime = "mcmc", chains = 4L, warmup_per_chain = 0L, thin = 1L, declarations = law$declarations)
postrank_diagnose(mc, pairs = data.frame(entity_i = "A", entity_j = "B", criterion_id = "k1"))$summaries$pair_1$diagnostics   # values: rhat 1.090465, ess_bulk 42.95484, mcse_mean 0.05764243 (1.0905, 42.95, .0576)

title: Uncertainty
text: Sampling error can move a unit to the top or bottom of a ranking, especially when its estimate is imprecise. The simulated league shows how often this happens. We then calculate the posterior probability of a direction for two units and for every pair in a probability matrix. The remaining examples compare ways to rank units, estimate how many statements a ranking gets wrong, and examine how Monte Carlo error affects those estimates. The pairwise probabilities enter the decision to assign ordered grades.

title: Majority comparisons and expected ranks
text: Counting pairs a unit more likely wins matches posterior-mean order under independent normal posteriors, yet diverges from expected rank and general laws.

title: Majority comparisons and expected ranks
text:
Numerical illustrations

Law on orders. A wins two pairs (.51 each); B’s .99 win puts B first by expected rank (1.52 vs. 1.98).
League. Majority wins match posterior means (0 of the 435 pairs differ); expected rank reverses 6 pairs (U13: 8th, 9.59 vs. 6th).
League, prior SD .30. Majority wins and posterior means differ on 0 of the 435 pairs; expected rank reverses 12 pairs.
KRW, race. Posterior mean reverses 35 of the 4,656 pairs (1,249 wrong) and expected rank 62; λ = 1 card reverses none (1,248).
KRW, gender. Macy’s (.5008), Jones Lang LaSalle (.502), and Dollar General (.5014) cycle at 45 pairs each; the card uses 96 grades.







Data: Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), doi:10.1257/aer.20230700; deposit doi:10.3886/E198284V1, CC-BY-NC, noncommercial use only (pr_case_krw; KRW’s cards along λ). No endorsement is implied. Data describe KRW’s experiment, not current conduct.

w <- rowSums(e < t(e), na.rm = TRUE); pm <- postrank_posterior_means(r)[, 1]; er <- postrank_expected_rank(r)
c(mean = sum(outer(w, w, ">") & outer(pm, pm, "<")), rank = sum(outer(w, w, ">") & outer(er, er, ">")))   # 35 62

title: Estimates and sampling error
text: Repeated samples add fresh random noise of standard deviation SE to a fixed true value, placing about two-thirds of estimates within one SE.

title: Estimates and sampling error
text:
Numerical illustrations

SE .20. Across 20 estimates of true value .50, 12 of 20 fall within one SE (vs. 13.7 expected); draw 20 gives .229 (.50 plus noise −.271).
200 draws. Over 200 draws, 132 of 200 fall within one SE against 137 expected (expected share .683).
Seed 2. A second sample places 18 of 20 estimates within one SE against the same 13.7 expected average.
SE .10. Halving the SE shrinks the noise arrow to −.136 while preserving standardized noise (−1.36 SEs) and 12 of 20 within one SE.
SE .05. Halving the SE again shrinks noise to −.0678 and keeps 12 of 20 within one SE.

title: Interval overlap across 435 pairs
text: Across all 435 pairs in the thirty-unit shrunk league, marginal credible intervals frequently overlap even when the posterior favors one direction with probability above .90.

title: Interval overlap across 435 pairs
text:
Numerical illustrations

Overlap, highest probability. 399 of 435 pairs overlap at 90%, and 88 favor one direction above .90 — led by U13 above U05 at .988 (overlap .00549).
U06 and U20. Intervals lie .00219 apart with Pr(U06 > U20) = .988, matching the top overlapping pair.
U04 and U18. Overlap .107 yet Pr(U04 > U18) = .904: U18 ends at −.105, below U04’s mean (−.0143).
95% intervals. 413 pairs overlap, 102 above .90, led by U03 above U15 at .997.
Prior SD .05. Stronger shrinkage yields 427 overlapping pairs, 58 above .90.



Probability bounds and source note

For two independent normal posteriors, whatever their SDs, the more likely direction has probability above .950 when their 90% intervals do not overlap, and at most .990 when they overlap (.975 and .997 for 95% intervals). Kline, Rose and Walters (2024, section IV.C) draw a credible interval beside each name, while grading names from pairwise posterior probabilities.

title: From data to posterior decisions
text: An analyst fits a model and prior to data Y to obtain Pr(θ ∣ Y); postrank acts only at the final step, turning that supplied posterior into grades.

title: From data to posterior decisions
text:
Numerical illustrations

Box 1 (Data). Y holds .25 (SE .10) for A and .05 (SE .20) for B.
Box 2 (Model). Prior SD .15 keeps .692 of A’s estimate and .360 of B’s.
Box 3 (Posterior). Means .173 and .0180 give π = .856; B more precise (SE .10) keeps .692, raising B to .0346 and π to .880.
Box 4 (Decision). {A} > {B} costs .144 vs. τ = .20 (best of all 3 reports); τ .10 withholds {A, B}.
Prior SD .05. Shrinks A to .0500 and π to .762 (error .238), withholding {A, B}.



Source notes (Walters; Kline, Rose and Walters, 2024)

Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), Section III.A–B, set out the empirical Bayes posteriors behind their firm grades (KRW call them beliefs). In their talk, slides 34 and 37 show the model for first names, not for the firms; slides 43 to 52 set out the empirical Bayes model for the firms. title: Sensitivity to the prior standard deviation
text: Varying the prior standard deviation from .01 to 1 across the simulated league shows that posterior means minimize squared error near the true spread while reshaping pairwise posterior probabilities.

title: Sensitivity to the prior standard deviation
text:
Numerical illustrations

Near the true spread. At prior SD .15 (true spread .149), mean squared error hits its grid minimum in this draw (.00958 vs. .0163 for estimates) and expected (.00754 vs. .0175; fine grid .146).
Much too narrow. At .02, overshrinking raises squared error above the estimates (.0197 vs. .0163 in this draw; .0191 vs. .0175 expected), and only 6 of the 435 pairs exceed .90.
Too narrow. At .05, squared error rises to .0148 (.0133 expected), expected misordered pairs reach 87.4, and 17 of 30 units end farther from truth.
Too wide. At .45, expected squared error matches .05 at .0133 (.0136 in this draw), yet 159 of the 435 pairs exceed .90 (45 exceed .99) and 13 units end farther.
Another draw. Under seed 20261031, this draw’s minimum moves to .12 (.00917), while expected squared error stays lowest at .15 (.00754).



Fixed-parameter experiment and source notes

The dashed curve (“expected”) gives the closed-form expected squared error across repeated estimate draws with the true values fixed — a fixed-parameter experiment in the postrank theory book (ch. 24, “Hyperparameters, precision and represented uncertainty”). postrank fits no model and takes the posterior it is given as input; whether high-probability directions hold under the true values is examined in Reported error and reference-law evaluation. Normal–normal shrinkage follows Walters’ Mixtape slides (p. 27).

title: Pairwise posterior direction probabilities
text: For two units A and B, π_AB = Pr(θ_A > θ_B ∣ Y) is the posterior probability that A’s true value exceeds B’s—the area above zero under the posterior of A − B.

title: Pairwise posterior direction probabilities
text:
Numerical illustrations

Means .30 and .10, SDs .20 and .20. π_AB = .760; difference SD .283 (.707 SDs above).
Means .30 and .10, SDs .20 and .60. Difference widens to SD .632 (.316 SDs above), lowering π_AB to .624.
Means .20 and .20, SDs .20 and .40. Equal means give π_AB = .500 (difference SD .447).
Means 1.20 and .95, SDs .20 and .20. Tutorial sites A and B give π_AB = .812.


Model assumptions and source notes
Under independent normal posteriors with positive SDs, the larger mean always gives π > .5 and πBA = 1 − πAB because equality has probability zero. Kline, Rose and Walters (2024), section II.E, Example 1, and slide 27 use the special case with both SDs equal to 1.

title: Selection bias at the extremes of a ranking
text: Selecting units with the largest estimates picks positive sampling errors on average; shrinking with a normal prior matched to the true spread removes nearly all of that upward bias.

title: Selection bias at the extremes of a ranking
text:
Numerical illustrations

Top 3. Across 2,000 replays, top-3 estimates average .160 above truth while posterior means at prior SD .15 (true SD .149) average −.00685; replay 1 gives .0709 and −.0308.
Replay 9. In replay 9 alone, top-3 estimates and posterior means differ from truth by −.0429 and −.117.
Top 1. Selecting only the single largest estimate raises average overshoot to .220 (vs. .0814 for k = 10), shrunk to −.0238.
Bottom 3. At the bottom end, estimates average −.150 from truth and posterior means average −.0132.
Prior SD .05. A prior narrower than the true spread overshrinks top-3 posterior means to −.131 (or −.0628 at prior SD .10).
